title: Can a planner beat selfish drivers?
hook: Every driver picks the faster road. Could a planner still make the average trip shorter?

knows: drivers pick the faster road (traffic equilibrium)
a road gets slower as more drivers use it
doesNotKnow: that the selfish equilibrium can be worse on average than a planner's split, by up to 4/3 with roads whose delay grows in proportion to traffic

misconception: If every driver picks the fastest route, the average trip is as short as it can be.
objective: The learner can explain that with road A at 60 min and road B at 60 min × its share, selfish drivers all take B and average 60 min, while a planner's half-and-half split averages 45 min, because each driver joining B slows everyone already on it; the ratio 4/3 is the worst case for delays proportional to traffic.

claims.text: With everyone on road B, the trip takes 60 minutes on both roads and no driver gains by switching; at any split with drivers on A, B is faster, so drivers on A want to switch.
claims.source: Road B delay = 60 × x for share x on B; road A = 60. For x < 1, 60x < 60, so a driver on A gains by moving; at x = 1 both are 60, so no one gains. Builder's node check (scratchpad ncmc/check.mjs), 2026-10-14. Matches brief cs.systems NCM #1 claim 1. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Own node check: B = 60x < 60 for every x < 1 (all 5% stops), equal at x = 1. Stage note text matches.

claims.text: Sending half the drivers to A cuts B to 30 minutes and the average trip to 45 minutes, the lowest any split reaches; an average of 30 is out of reach because drivers on A still take 60. The reveal quotes the lowest average among the splits the learner visited.
claims.source: avg(x) = (1 - x)·60 + x·60x, derivative 120x - 60 = 0 at x = 0.5, avg = 45; builder grid over 0..100 in steps of 5 (2026-10-14). Avg 30 would need everyone at 30 or below, but A is fixed at 60 and B reaches 30 only at x = 0.5. v3: the 'Half on each' button and the QA path reach 50% (milestone found-best). | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own grid 0..100 step 5: avg(50) = 45 is the unique minimum (45.15 at 45 and 55). B at 50% = 30. found-best is required, so the reveal's best = 50 and ', where B takes 30' always prints. Avg >= 45 > 30 everywhere.

claims.text: Of 100 drivers, at 50% on B the next 5 to join B each save 27 minutes (135 in all), while the 50 already on B each lose 3 minutes (150 in all): the joiners feel their gain, and nobody choosing feels the loss.
claims.source: Demo.tsx joinCost(50): B goes from 30 to 33 min, so each joiner saves 60 - 33 = 27 (x5 = 135); each B driver loses 60·5/100 = 3 (x50 = 150). Check: 100·(avg(55) - avg(50)) = 15 = 150 - 135 (builder's Node run, 2026-10-14). The stage line and the reveal quote the last split visited between 5% and 95%, computed by the same function. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own joinCost(50): after 33, 27 each, 135 in all; 50 x 3 = 150; 100 x (avg 55 - avg 50) = 15. Non-blocking for the builder: the reveal quotes the LAST split visited, and below 50% the joiners' gain beats the loss (20%: 225 vs 60), so 'The line under the chart is why' does not show the waste there. Every sentence is still true.

claims.text: With delays that are a fixed time plus a part proportional to traffic, the selfish equilibrium's total travel time is at most 4/3 of the best possible, and this two-road example reaches that bound.
claims.source: Roughgarden T. & Tardos É. (2002), 'How bad is selfish routing?', J. ACM 49(2): price of anarchy 4/3 for linear (affine) latency functions, attained by Pigou's two-link example (Pigou 1920, The Economics of Welfare). Easley & Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 8. Attribution for the fact-checker to confirm. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): DISPUTED (wording of the class). Roughgarden & Tardos ('How bad is selfish routing?', FOCS 2000 / J. ACM 2002) prove the 4/3 bound for linear (affine) latencies a*x + b; confirmed by web search snippet only, paper PDF blocked. But the sentence says 'delays that grow in proportion to traffic', and road A (constant 60) is not proportional; with purely proportional delays a*x, equilibrium equals optimum (marginal cost 2ax is proportional to delay), so the example would not be in the stated class. Fix (builder, reveal and claim): 'With delays that are a fixed time plus a part proportional to traffic, that is the worst it can ever be.' | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, W-193): Was 'delays that grow in proportion to traffic'. Reveal and claim now name the affine class (fixed time plus a part proportional to traffic), per the fact-checker's fix. Needs an independent check. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Reveal wording now 'a fixed time plus a part proportional to traffic' (affine). Bound re-derived: Wardrop equilibrium f satisfies sum l(f)f <= sum l(f)f*; for l = ax + b, l(f)f* <= l(f*)f* + a f^2/4 <= l(f*)f* + l(f)f/4, so C(f) <= (4/3) C(f*). Example: 60/45 = 4/3, so it attains the bound. Roughgarden-Tardos not opened; not relied on.

claims.text: Road A always takes 60 min; road B takes 60 min × its share of drivers.
claims.source: Stage set-up (Demo.tsx A_MIN, timeB), from the brief. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Demo A_MIN = 60, timeB(pct) = 60*pct/100; predict question states the same.

recall.question: Drivers choose freely between a fixed-time road and a road that gets slower with traffic. Compared with the best possible split, their average trip is…
options: Longer: each driver ignores the delay they add for others
The same: free choice finds the best split
Shorter: drivers know their own trips best
recall.why: At the selfish equilibrium no single driver can gain by switching, but each one who crowds the variable road slows everyone on it. A planner who holds some drivers back on the fixed road lowers the average; with linear delays the selfish cost is at most 4/3 of the best.
